subjects.displayTitle: Prayer at the edge of understanding
subjects.introduction: How shall I call upon Thee, and how shall I not? The Báb lets both questions stand in one breath: every supplication falls back upon the soul that offered it, and yet the heart, enraptured with love, cannot stay silent. Reason says make no mention of Him, for He is sanctified above all remembrance; love says speak. Worship lives in that tension. The Essence of God cannot be praised as it deserves by any creature kneaded from limitation and need, and the Writings go so far as to call even the cry of ‘Hallowed art Thou’ a venture to describe the indescribable. Still the servant worships through the watches of the night, as the mind’s failure becomes the honest shape of devotion. Pseudo-Dionysius carries praise past both affirmation and denial in his own Christian account of transcendence, a discipline worth setting beside these confessions without merging the two [1]. What remains possible is recognition rather than comprehension: God is known through His signs, His revealed Word and the qualities shown forth in His Manifestations, and a prayer can be sincere without pretending to be complete. The path from here leads into the unknowability of God, the limits of the intellect, and the living state of prayer where humility turns into love.
subjects.arc: Begin with the heart’s paradox, distinguish recognition from comprehension of the Essence, and return to prayer as a response shaped by love and humility.

order.why: Follow the limits placed upon description.
Open with the tension between inability to call and inability to remain silent.
shortened: O my God! How shall I call upon Thee, when the utmost end of my supplication returns unto my own soul, plaintive over the vile deeds I have wrought? And how shall I not call upon Thee, when my heart hath been ever enraptured with Thy love, unable to endure Thy separation, to be silent from communion with Thee, or to remain far from the seats of Thy nearness?

order.why: Hear the same tension between reasoning and the loving heart.
shortened: How can I make mention of Thee after realizing that any remembrance of aught else but Thee befitteth not Thy presence? And how can I fail to make mention of Thee when I find within my heart the love of Thy beauty? Reason saith: Make no mention of Him, for He hath ever been sanctified above the remembrance of all beings and exalted beyond the recognition of all creatures.

order.why: Let love accompany the confession of inadequate worship.
shortened: I love Thee and worship Thee though I have neither the power nor the knowledge to do so as befitteth Thee. Glorified and exalted art Thou! Thy Reality is sanctified and Thine Identity is exalted above being known by anyone through anything save Thine Own Essence, and mighty is Thine Identity.

order.why: Introduce the interplay of justice, grace, fear, and hope.
Read the acknowledgement that worship has not fulfilled its object.
shortened: Here I stand in this station, confessing my powerlessness and shortcoming. I have not known Thee as Thou makest Thyself known to me, nor have I worshipped Thee as Thou callest me to worship Thee.

order.why: Discusses the limits of worship and knowledge in contingent being and the problem of separating God from His manifestation.
Keep ceaseless remembrance beside the limits of praise.
Consider the distance between utterance and divine might.
shortened: How can I move my lips in remembrance of Thee when I know that my remembrance and my existence are as nothing in the presence of the manifestations of Thy sovereign might and nonexistent before the revelations of Thy holy eternity?

order.why: Read the question of remembrance ascending to God.
Place devotional poverty within an ordeal.
Read the movement of refuge toward God.
Distinguish worship from comprehending the Essence.
shortened: None hath worshipped Him in a manner befitting His holy Essence. Every being that hath desired to love His Essence hath been rejected before God and all creation, for it hath sought the impossible.

order.why: Explore why created descriptions cannot encompass their source.
Consider the contrast between created language and eternity.
Read attributes as denying imperfection rather than defining the Essence.
shortened: The purpose is to show that these attributes and perfections that we recount for that Universal Reality are only in order to deny imperfections, rather than to assert the perfections that the human mind can conceive. Thus we say His attributes are unknowable.
In fine, that Universal Reality with all its qualities and attributes that we recount is holy and exalted above all minds and understandings.

order.why: Revisit that distinction in a concise formulation.
shortened: We affirm these names and attributes not to affirm the perfections of God but to deny that He has any imperfections.

order.why: Retain the detailed interpretation of divine unity.
shortened: Know thou that in Sufi exegesis it is affirmed, with respect to the Unseen Esence [ghayb-i huwiyyat] in the station of Primal Oneness,  that all names are far from the shore of Its Sanctity and It is known without Name or Attribute.  For the Names of the Absolute  are the reflections of [Its] Attributes and the Attributes of the Absolute in that station of Primal Oneness are the same as its Essence  without a trace of difference or distinction -- it is even as that King of the Court of Knowledge and Wisdom and that Monarch of the Kingdom of Divine Guidance, His Holiness 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (unto him be greetings and praise) has stated:  "Perfect belief in Divine Unity consists in the denial of all His Attributes."

order.why: Read the language of inadequacy as a devotional confession.
shortened: O my God! Given such clear and evident powerlessness, such plain and manifest poverty in recognizing the least of the signs of Thy dominion in the world of creation, how then can I unloose my tongue to make mention of Thine attributes and to proclaim Thy virtues? How can I speak forth Thy praise and celebrate Thy glory in Thy presence?
For to proclaim Thy sanctity and holiness is naught but to venture to describe Thee and, as such, is an evident sin, a shameful and palpable error.

order.why: Distinguish divine independence from human obedience.
Consider worship according to created capacities.
shortened: How then can one who has no way to comprehend the essence of knowing Thine eternity possibly worship Thee? Glorified art Thou above this, and exalted art Thou beyond that! All worship Thee according to what Thou hast created in them of the likeness of Thy creation, and all unite in Thy oneness through what Thou hast deposited within them of the signs of Thy handiwork.

order.why: Examine the inadequacy of even claims to complete detachment.
Read nearness as acknowledging the limits of love and knowledge.
shortened: While all draw nigh unto Thee through their love for Thee, I draw nigh unto Thee through my acknowledgment that I do not truly love Thee, for this is impossible for anyone. Had I found the way and discovered the proof, by Thy glory, I would have been the first of interpreters. But after recognizing my limitations and observing the nothingness of my existence, how can I clothe falsehood in truth or vest the contingent with the Absolute?

order.why: Keep the intense language of nothingness within its devotional setting.
shortened: Glorified is He! I bear witness that there is no God but Him, as He is, without any being able to know how He is, though I know my very existence is pure sin before Him - how then could my testimony of Him be worthy? Existence itself is steeped in sin and cannot indicate God. So glory be to God, though I know all paths are cut off; praise be to God, though I recognize all ways are blocked; God is Most Great, though I witness the impossibility of all records.

order.why: Distinguish revealed names from possession of the Essence.
Read the further warning about names and attribution.
shortened: Whoso worshippeth God through any of His attributes or names hath disbelieved in Him and hath worshipped naught. And whoso turneth unto Him through any of His servants hath not turned unto Him, and the face of His might veils him from beholding His countenance.

order.why: Consider recognition through the revealed Word.
shortened: All worship Thee, yet none worshippeth Thee as beseemeth Thy due. Indeed this utterance of mine is raised up to Thee through the Dawning-Place of Thy Self, where all worship Thee according to what Thou hast revealed in the Bayan.

order.why: Turn toward the signs by which recognition becomes possible.
Preserve room for rational deduction within acknowledged limits.
Move from limited self-knowledge to a request for greater knowledge of signs.
shortened: O my God! The nearest of Thy signs to my soul is my own soul, and my soul's inability to know its own true essence is among the most self-evident facts to my soul.

Therefore I beseech Thee, O my God, by Thy signs and the effulgence of Thy grace and Thy mercy and Thy guidance, to expand my breast through knowledge of Thy signs in Thy Book and in Thy earth and Thy heaven, and especially the Seven Oft-repeated Verses and the Great Qur'an.

order.why: Examine different motives for worship.
shortened: Some worship Thee for what Thou givest them; some ask Thee for the needs they desire; some abandon the world and sever themselves from its pleasures, yet forsake Thy good-pleasure in the world to come; some obey Thee out of fear; some worship Thee out of love; some affirm Thy unity because Thy oneness is nobler than all things; and some remember Thee because Thy remembrance is more manifest than every remembrance.

order.why: Keep the polemical warning against religious attribution concealing wrongdoing.
Return to remembrance and the names of the Beloved.
Close the linked readings with the limits of private and public prayer.
shortened: I know not how to call upon Thee or remember Thee, for whenever I remember Thee among the congregation, the limit of contingent being frightens me in my heart, and whenever I worship Thee in solitude, the ultimate bound of creation rebukes me openly, saying that the servant can never know Thee and Thou canst not be described by him. Thou canst never be worshipped as Thou deserves to be worshipped, and none knoweth how Thou art except Thee alone.

order.why: Compare the supplied Plotinian account while preserving its attribution.
Read the supplied Dionysian passage as a distinct tradition of negation.
End with the provisional prayer concerning worship through God.

questions: What makes prayer meaningful when the worshipper acknowledges its inadequacy?
How do the passages distinguish knowing God’s signs from comprehending the divine Essence?
When does religious language deepen understanding, and when might it conceal its own limits?
How does the comparison with Pseudo-Dionysius illuminate both shared questions and different accounts of approaching God?
What forms of inquiry, attention, or conduct might grow from the humility expressed in these prayers?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the capacities and limits of human inquiry.

references.label: 1 · Pseudo-Dionysius, Mystical Theology, V · Beyond affirmation and denial
references.note: Chapter V carries its negations beyond sensible images and intellectual concepts, then beyond affirmation and denial themselves. Compare that discipline with the compilation’s confessions of inadequate praise. The Christian work’s account of mystical union should be considered alongside, rather than equated with, the distinctions concerning the divine Essence here. Translation by the editors of The Shrine of Wisdom (1923).

subjects.displayTitle: What lasts: love, service, and the passing world
subjects.introduction: Everything now visible will soon vanish, Bahá’u’lláh writes, but a single sigh breathed for the love of God endures for ever and shows its effects in all the worlds. The scale is deliberately lopsided: one breath against kingdoms. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá goes looking for men among the palaces, since buildings are many and men are few, and reminds the builder laying a foundation that a day will come when not one stone remains; a book may carry a name for a thousand years and then be forgotten, while a deed done in God’s path outlasts the cycles. Joy and sorrow pass alike, crowns turn to dust, and the governor who protected Bahá’u’lláh for a few days left a single brick in the City of God when all his villages were gone. What lasts is service to others, recognition, and love, and the nightingale sings only in spring, so the present is urgent. Jesus set treasure that moth and rust corrupt against treasure in heaven and tied the treasure to the direction of the heart [1]. The road continues into life and death, the cycles of the physical and spiritual worlds, the meaning of infinity and eternity, and the worthlessness assigned to the physical world when it is loved for itself.
subjects.arc: Open with the disproportionate worth of love, face the transience of possessions and feeling, and follow service toward the compilation’s accounts of enduring life.

order.why: Read consolation after the loss of a house.
shortened: As to lofty buildings, imposing mansions, and magnificent palaces: Every inhabited and flourishing place will become desolate and every mighty edifice reduced to ruin. Therefore, how much better it is for these habitations which are more fragile than a spider's web to be wrecked and ruined for the love of the sovereign Lord of the Kingdom. For if a house of clay be destroyed, there will be reared in its stead a glorious mansion within the soul-uplifting immensity of the realms above. If one's home and dwelling-place be laid waste in this transitory dust-heap, one will be provided with a matchless and incomparable nest within the rose-garden of eternity.

order.why: Open with one loving breath outweighing what vanishes.
shortened: That which exists and is witnessed shall soon vanish, but any deed performed by any soul for the triumph of God's Cause, even if it be but a sigh breathed forth for the love of God, shall endure forever and its effects shall be manifested in all the divine worlds through wondrous and sublime appearances.

order.why: Give enduring worth a practical test in benefit to all.
Consider talent directed toward service.
shortened: If we spend our talent in the Cause of God its outcome will be everlasting, but if we waste it over worldly affairs, it is like drawing pictures over the surface of the water. For example if we write a book, it may perpetuate our name for a thousand or two thousand years, it will be forgotten afterwards. But if he breaths one breath in the path of God, it will immortalize him throughout ages and cycles.

order.why: Let the passing season make present opportunity urgent.
shortened: Drink from the wine of love and close thine eyes to the world, for whatever thou seest will perish and pass away in an instant, while that which is with God remaineth and perisheth not, and endureth and fadeth not away. Know the value of these days, for union is not always possible. The nightingale singeth only in spring and crieth not until it seeth the rose. The time cometh when the divine nightingale ceaseth from mentioning meanings and taketh flight to the spiritual branch and settleth in the divine invisible rose gardens.

order.why: Remember that sorrow as well as joy passes.
Read the reported image of the world as theatre.
shortened: Another time the Bahai Master said: "This world is a theatre. It is not an eternal world: it is a stage where every kind of play is enacted.

order.why: Contrast worldly ornaments with lasting spiritual comfort.
shortened: The crown which is luminous with gems will be changed to a coronet of dust and the canopy on the beds which are cossetted with feathers and silk will be changed to dark earth - except the honor of the All-Merciful One and the comforts which are based on the spirit, these are eternal and everlasting.

order.why: Extend the contrast to names, traces, and ease.
shortened: Every name and trace shall be erased and obliterated, and every comfort and ease shall ultimately be transformed into trials.

order.why: Consider the disappearance of kings and persistence of spiritual traces.
shortened: One must attain eternal life and seek everlasting sovereignty.
Consider carefully that millions of kings came into this world and all were obliterated and disappeared.
Even in this transient world his traces remain firm and enduring, his mention continues, and his light spreads.

order.why: Turn from palaces to the cultivation of human beings.
shortened: Buildings are many, men are few. There are ever so many palaces in the world. There have been great palaces built by the ancient Kings and to day not a stone has been left to tell the sad story of their fall. The present palaces will go through the same process of decline.
But the divine Palace shall never be destroyed, its traces are eternal.

order.why: Retain the reported historical example in its own terms.
shortened: Mu'tamidu'd-Dawlih of Isfahan, Manuchihr Khan, built extensively. He owned many villages around Tehran. All these edifices, these buildings, these properties - all of them vanished. All of it was ruined, no trace remained. However, in the City of God he laid one brick, and that brick endured and will not be destroyed. For several days he protected the Blessed Beauty from enemies in his private quarters. At first he outwardly sent Him away but then kept Him protected in his private covered quarters. This brick he laid in the City of God, and it will never be destroyed. This trace of his will remain forever in the divine edifice.

order.why: Read the specific offering of hair within the promise of spiritual gifts.
shortened: And though it be thine hair that thou hast sacrificed, yet thou shalt be filled with the Spirit, and though it be this perishable member of thy body which thou hast laid down in the path of God, yet thou shalt find the Divine Gift, shalt behold the Celestial Beauty, obtain imperishable glory and attain unto everlasting life.

order.why: Consider the apostolic image of shelter beyond earthly possession.
shortened: Christ and the Holy Manifestations and the apostles had no nest whatsoever in this ephemeral world, yet in the divine realm they had a mighty palace.

order.why: Compare earthly kingship with spiritual sovereignty.
Distinguish stable sovereignty from fancy.
shortened: But thou hast an enduring and steadfast sovereignty. Herein lies the difference: the might of that sovereignty is but fancy and imagination, while the glory of this sovereignty is the opening chapter of divine favors and its blessed conclusion.

order.why: Explore servitude as a paradoxical sovereignty.
shortened: But the servitude of the servants of God is an eternal sovereignty - as ages and cycles pass, its flame grows brighter and its rays become more luminous.

order.why: Locate honour in serving the friends.
shortened: But the magnet of divine bestowals is service to the friends and servitude to the loved ones, for the results of the aforementioned occupations end in buried graves and produce unappreciated hardships and difficulties. However, the grateful servant of the friends attains eternal glory and finds everlasting bounty.

order.why: Read enduring names in relation to righteousness.
Consider deeds described as remaining.
shortened: Soon shalt thou behold its effects in the seat of truth with the mighty King, for worldly rewards are temporary, but "the good deeds that endure are best in thy Lord's sight as rewards and best as works to merit."

order.why: Read action through the image of a lasting fragrance.
shortened: Blessed is the soul that in this transient world hath attained unto that which is everlasting - that is, such deeds as shed forth the fragrance of eternity, and these have been and ever shall be the Word of God.

order.why: Follow the promise of enduring deeds.
shortened: The deeds and actions of such souls have endured and shall endure for as long as the kingdom of earth and heaven endure.

order.why: Connect lasting worth with the direction of aspiration.
shortened: However, whatever pertains to the physical world is illusory and consists of transient reflections, for it yields no result, bears no fruit, and does not endure. Its difficulty ends in ease, and its ease concludes in difficulty.
That which is lasting and enduring is worthy of consideration and deserving of the righteous ones' aspiration.

order.why: Contrasts the passing pleasures and honors of this life with the pursuit of what endures.
Read spiritual inheritance amid changing circumstances.
Consider the station that remains when things pass.
shortened: All that is in the world shall perish and pass away, while this most exalted and glorious station shall endure for thee eternally.

order.why: Place remembrance within the divine kingdom.
Ask how true life is defined in the reported passage.
Connect enduring life with recognition.
shortened: But the true ocean remains fixed and stable. Though its waves may be great and terrible, they swiftly disappear. Though thunder and lightning may be severe, they vanish in the twinkling of an eye. What is eternal is the soul of the people of recognition.

order.why: Consider revelation as a source of life.
Read the invitation to hasten toward that life.
Keep consolation and grace together.
shortened: Therefore do not be sorrowful, do not be grieved. Find comfort in His endless grace and the glad-tidings of eternal life.

order.why: Follow love toward an eternal horizon.
shortened: However, your countenance shall become radiant in the celestial paradise and your love shall become bright and luminous in the eternal world.

order.why: Read the reviving image of divine breezes.
Pause at the image of spring without autumn.
shortened: The joy-giving garden is the Abha Paradise, whose spring has no autumn and whose April has no winter following. The eternal beauty and divine countenance undergo no change or alteration.

order.why: Distinguish conditioned existence from the unconditioned.
Keep the distinction between temporal and eternal natures.
Consider how relation to Truth changes the language of endurance.
shortened: Whatever is attributed to the Truth is beloved and desired, and is joined with eternality and immortality; and whatever pertains to creation is ephemeral and transient, detested and condemned.

order.why: Retain the reported Elijah comparison without turning it into an independent historical claim.
shortened: That which endures are the institutions of God's loved ones; divine foundations are eternal. Two thousand five hundred years ago, Elijah dwelt here in a cave. Some days he would ascend the mountain and rest in the shade of this cave. Now after two thousand five hundred years it has become this magnificent monastery. But consider how many kings have come and gone in this period, what trials they endured, yet perished, while the cave where Elijah occasionally went to rest remains.

order.why: Read the paradox of annihilation and permanence as spiritual self-effacement.

questions: What kinds of worth do these passages distinguish from wealth, fame, or duration alone?
How might the recognition that both joy and sorrow pass change our response to the present?
What connects service to others with the compilation’s language of enduring life?
How does Matthew’s association of treasure with the heart compare with the motives examined here?
How do the passages of consolation, exhortation, and philosophical distinction alter one another when read together?

references.label: 1 · Matthew 6:19–21 · Treasure and the heart
references.note: Jesus contrasts possessions vulnerable to decay and theft with treasure in heaven, linking the location of treasure to the orientation of the heart. Compare this with the compilation’s accounts of love and service that endure. The analogy invites reflection on priorities without requiring identical explanations of eternal life.

subjects.displayTitle: Philosophy that becomes a way of life
subjects.introduction: Science, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, is the highest attainment on the human plane, and it comes in two kinds: the material, which investigates natural phenomena, and the divine, which discovers spiritual verities. A bird cannot fly on one wing. Natural philosophy has served humanity magnificently; divine philosophy, whose object is the ennobling of human nature, has been outdistanced and neglected. A philosophy that stops at the five senses, He observes with a straight face, is a station the cow has reached without twenty years of study. He honours Socrates poisoned for believing in one God and an immortal soul, and argues sharply with Mullá Sadrá, in conversations whose terms deserve to be read in their setting. The real test is whether thought becomes life, as it does in a teacher who is the first to practise his own teaching. Epictetus asked the same of his students, to digest their principles and show them in conduct rather than boast of them [1]. From here the way leads to the Greek philosophers, to the two kinds of knowledge, acquired and immediate, and to the difference between sight and insight.
subjects.arc: Begin with the two wings of inquiry, explore the questions and historical debates of divine philosophy, and bring knowledge back to education, unity, and lived example.

order.why: Read the sustained appeal for reason, science, and the cultivation of virtues.
shortened: Philosophy is of two kinds: natural and divine. Natural philosophy seeks knowledge of physical verities and explains material phenomena, whereas divine philosophy deals with ideal verities and phenomena of the spirit.

Now is the time for us to make an effort and enable it to advance apace with the philosophy of material investigation so that awakening of the ideal virtues may progress equally with the unfoldment of the natural powers. In the same proportion that the body of man is developing, the spirit of man must be strengthened; and just as his outer perceptions have been quickened, his inner intellectual powers must be sensitized so that he need not rely wholly upon tradition and human precedent. In divine questions we must not depend entirely upon the heritage of tradition and former human experience; nay, rather, we must exercise reason, analyze and logically examine the facts presented so that confidence will be inspired and faith attained.

order.why: Open with natural and spiritual knowledge as two wings.
shortened: It is of two kinds: material and spiritual. Material science is the investigation of natural phenomena; divine science is the discovery and realization of spiritual verities. The world of humanity must acquire both. A bird has two wings; it cannot fly with one. Material and spiritual science are the two wings of human uplift and attainment.

order.why: Define philosophy as inquiry within human capacity.
shortened: Philosophy consists in comprehending, so far as human power permits, the realities of things as they are in themselves.

order.why: Bring both kinds of learning into education.
Distinguish the educational scope attributed to philosophers and Manifestations.
shortened: Teachers are of two kinds: universal and special. The universal Instructors are the Prophets of God, and the special teachers are the philosophers. The philosophers are capable of educating and training a limited circle of human souls, whereas the holy, divine Manifestations of God confer general education upon humanity.

order.why: Distinguish conceptual knowledge from realization.
Introduce inward reflection beside public discourse.
shortened: They divided Divine philosophy into two parts: one kind is that of which the knowledge can be acquired through lectures and study in schools and colleges. The second kind of philosophy was that of the Illuminati, or followers of the inner light. The schools of this philosophy were held in silence.

Some of the great questions unfolding from the rays of the Sun of Reality upon the mind of man are: the problem of the reality of the spirit of man; of the birth of the spirit; of its birth from this world into the world of God; the question of the inner life of the spirit and of its fate after its ascension from the body.
They go so far as to reflect upon the essential nature of the Divinity, of the Divine revelation, of the manifestation of the Deity in this world.

order.why: Consider the intellect’s access to realities beyond sense perception.
Read the specified critique of materialism without extending it to all philosophers.
shortened: By materialists, whose belief with regard to Divinity hath been explained, is not meant philosophers in general, but rather that group of materialists of narrow vision who worship that which is sensed, who depend upon the five senses only, and whose criterion of knowledge is limited to that which can be perceived by the senses. All that can be sensed is to them real, whilst whatever falleth not under the power of the senses is either unreal or doubtful. The existence of the Deity they regard as wholly doubtful.

order.why: Keep the historical East–West categories within their setting.
Examine the competing accounts of nature.
shortened: The materialists hold to the opinion that the world of nature is complete. The divine philosophers declare that the world of nature is incomplete. There is a wide difference between the two. The materialists call attention to the perfection of nature, the sun, moon and stars, the trees in their adornment, the whole earth and the sea -- even unimportant phenomena revealing the most perfect symmetry.

order.why: Consider perception and volition in the argument about ultimate reality.
shortened: The philosophers also each say that a force or universal reality is the source of all created things. Their difference with the Prophets is only in this: that the Prophets say that universal reality and all-encompassing aspect is the absolutely wealthy, perceiving and choosing by will, while the philosophers consider it poor, non-perceiving and powerless.

order.why: Read the argument concerning the soul’s immortality.
Distinguish different uses of paradise and hell.
shortened: In the heavenly books mention is made of the immortality of the spirit, which is the very foundation of the divine religions. For rewards and punishments are said to be of two kinds, one being existential rewards and punishments and the other, ultimate rewards and punishments. Existential paradise and hell are to be found in all the worlds of God, whether in this world or in the heavenly realms of the spirit, and to gain these rewards is to attain life eternal.

order.why: Follow the reported account of matter through the kingdoms.
shortened: As each component atom or element in the physical organisms of existence is subject to transference through endless forms and stages, possessing virtues peculiar to those forms and stations, it is evident that all phenomena of material being are fundamentally one. In the mineral kingdom this component atom or element possesses certain virtues of the mineral; in the kingdom of the vegetable it is imbued with vegetable qualities or virtues; in the plane of animal existence it is empowered with animal virtues -- the senses; and in the kingdom of man it manifests qualities peculiar to the human station.

order.why: Read elemental transformation without treating it as a doctrine of personal reincarnation.
shortened: Man is indestructible. The man you see before your eyes has travelled through all the worlds of existence. Those molecular atoms which go into the make-up of the human body were originally in the mineral world, and these atoms have had journeyings and coursings through all the various phases of the mineral kingdom, appearing under various forms and images.

In brief these primordial atoms have coursings and transferences in infinite images. In every image they had a certain peculiar virtue. Therefore, these primordial atoms, which have now appeared in man, have had myriads of transferences in phenomena, and in each degree appearing with certain virtue and function.

order.why: Retain the report connecting natural philosophy and Persian philosophical discussions.
Keep the extended philosophical polemic and historical claims visibly attributed.
shortened: The metaphysical concepts of Mulla Sadra and Muhyi'd-Din are largely fanciful. For instance, the concept of the Universal Spirit is but fancy and imagination, not reality. For example, Mulla Sadra's ten intellects were derived from the idol-worshipping Greek philosophers.

Man is distinguished from all created things; nature - all things are its captive. The sun, for all its greatness, is its captive. But man, whose body is so small, God hath created within him a sacred power that can break the laws of nature.
From the first day of Mulla Sadra until this day, what result hath been achieved?

order.why: Consider the hope for discoveries surpassing earlier attainment.
Read encouragement to study philosophy.
shortened: In the Tablets of His Holiness Baha'Ullah, there are many philosophic questions.
In His Tablets He has encouraged and rather urged (the people) to study philosophy. Therefore, in the region of Baha'Ullah philosophy is highly esteemed.

order.why: Distinguish examining a question from adopting every belief discussed.
Consider philosophy’s contribution to developing the mind.
Connect heavenly science with the fruit of life.
Read the aspiration toward a philosophy consonant with spiritual reality.
Consider the reported call to bring natural and divine philosophy into conformity.
Argues that schools should combine divine and natural philosophy rather than teach material subjects alone.
Follow the contrast through the image of a heavenly bird.
Keep the satirical cow comparison within the critique of sensory restriction.
Read the further reported polemic as a historical argument.
Retain the reported contrast between understanding and formal learning.
Bring knowledge into the cultivation of human capacities.
shortened: The mission of the Prophets, the revelation of the Holy Books, the manifestation of the heavenly Teachers and the purpose of divine philosophy all center in the training of the human realities so that they may become clear and pure as mirrors and reflect the light and love of the Sun of Reality.

order.why: Place the unity of humanity among philosophy’s concerns.
shortened: The most important principle of divine philosophy is the oneness of the world of humanity, the unity of mankind, the bond conjoining East and West, the tie of love which blends human hearts.

order.why: Consider the challenge to beautiful language without corresponding conduct.
shortened: The greatest philosophers without this Spirit are powerless, their souls lifeless, their hearts dead! Unless the Holy Spirit breathes into their souls, they can do no good work.
Learned philosophers, unenlightened by the Divine Spirit, have often been men of inferior morality; they have not proclaimed in their actions the reality of their beautiful phrases.
The difference between spiritual philosophers and others is shown by their lives.

order.why: Close the linked readings with teachers practising their own ideals.
Read the fuller supplied account of knowledge contradicted by behaviour.
shortened: This is the difference between philosophers who are Spiritual Teachers, and those who are mere philosophers: the Spiritual Teacher is the first to follow His own teaching; He brings down into the world of action His spiritual conceptions and ideals.

When we find a philosopher emphasizing the importance and grandeur of justice, and then encouraging a rapacious monarch in his oppression and tyranny, we quickly realize that he belongs to the first class: for he thinks heavenly thoughts and does not practise the corresponding heavenly virtues. This state is impossible with Spiritual Philosophers, for they ever express their high and noble thoughts in actions.

order.why: Introduce the supplied Platonic reflection on philosophy and death.
Consider Plato’s argument about soul and order.
End with the supplied account of the soul’s pursuit of understanding.

questions: How do natural inquiry and spiritual understanding assist or question one another in these selections?
What distinguishes possessing a concept from allowing an insight to change one’s life?
How might we examine the historical arguments about materialism fairly while retaining their concern with human purpose?
What does Epictetus’s test of philosophy through conduct add to the demand that teachers practise their ideals?
What would an education joining rigorous inquiry, moral growth, and the unity of humanity look like?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the relation between acquired knowledge and insight.

references.label: 1 · Epictetus, Enchiridion, 46 · Showing philosophy through conduct
references.note: In section 46, Epictetus asks the learner to digest principles and let their effects appear in action instead of boasting of philosophical learning. Compare this with the selections on the teacher’s example and knowledge put into practice. The shared ethical test does not erase differences between Stoic philosophy and the compilation’s account of revelation. Elizabeth Carter translation.

subjects.displayTitle: Being and nonbeing: dependence, change, and reality
subjects.introduction: A chair has a carpenter, a piece of wood, a shape and a purpose, and so it owes its being to causes; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins with something that ordinary, because the question it opens is anything but. Does a thing that depends on a cause exist less? He answers that existence and nonexistence are relative terms: the mineral is nothing compared with a human being, yet it is fully real in its own kingdom, and the world is a mirage beside God while remaining established and undeniable in its own degree. He separates a beginning in time from dependence on a cause, as the moon’s light is derived from the sun without the sun having once shone alone, and he insists that absolute nothingness could never become anything at all. Augustine saw the same distinction in a song, whose sound is its material without ever being heard first as formless noise [1]. The vocabulary then shifts register: in prayer, nothingness is no longer a philosophical category but the honest confession of a creature before its Creator, and dependence turns into gratitude. The inquiry carries on into necessary and possible being, into the strange permanence of elementary matter that is never annihilated, and into the mystical passing away and abiding that the Sufis call fana and baqa.
subjects.arc: Begin with familiar examples of causal dependence, distinguish relative nonbeing from absolute absence, and follow the changing vocabulary into prayer and spiritual life.

order.why: State that the world is real in its own degree.
shortened: The sophists hold that all existence is illusory, indeed, that each and every being is an absolute illusion that has no existence whatsoever--in other words, that the existence of created things is like a mirage, or like the reflection of an image in water or in a mirror, which is merely an appearance devoid of any basis, foundation or ascertainable reality.
This notion is false, for although the existence of things is an illusion compared to the existence of God, yet in the contingent world it is established, proven, and undeniable.
It is therefore evident that although created things have no existence compared to that of God, being instead like a mirage or an image reflected in a mirror, yet in their own degree they exist.

order.why: Open with a chair and the distinction between temporal and essential origination.
shortened: Essential pre-existence is an existence which is not preceded by a cause; essential origination is preceded by a cause. Temporal pre-existence has no beginning; temporal origination has both a beginning and an end. For the existence of each and every thing depends upon four causes: the efficient cause, the material cause, the formal cause and the final cause. So this chair has a creator who is a carpenter, a matter which is wood, a form which is that of a chair, and a purpose which is to serve as a seat. Therefore, this chair is essentially originated, for it is preceded by, and its existence is conditioned upon, a cause.

order.why: Use borrowed moonlight to examine dependence.
shortened: Answer: Pre-existence is of two kinds. One is essential pre-existence, which is not preceded by a cause but which exists in itself. For example, the sun shines in itself and does not depend on the radiance of the other stars for its light. This is called essential light. But the light of the moon is derived from the sun, for the moon is in need of the sun for its radiance. Thus, with respect to light, the sun is the cause and the moon the effect. The former is ancient, antecedent and prior, while the latter is preceded by something else.

order.why: Develop the distinction between essence and existence.
Consider beginningless creation alongside divine independence.
Distinguish the soul’s continuance from absolute existence.
shortened: When the soul attaineth the Presence of God, it will assume the form that best befitteth its immortality and is worthy of its celestial habitation. Such an existence is a contingent and not an absolute existence, inasmuch as the former is preceded by a cause, whilst the latter is independent thereof. Absolute existence is strictly confined to God, exalted be His glory.

order.why: Read the statement of divine transcendence beyond chronological limitation.
shortened: This is the same word which declareth "God was, and there was nothing else besides Him" and He shall be as He hath ever been. Every person of insight testifieth that the Lord now existeth while that which is lorded over is non-existent - meaning that His sacred realm transcendeth all else, and whatsoever is mentioned in the realm of contingent being is limited by contingent limitations, while the Truth is sanctified therefrom.

order.why: Explore existence as derived rather than identical with essence.
Distinguish a predicated concept of existence from the doctrine being discussed.
shortened: Those pre-eminent Sufis who founded the doctrine of the "unity of existence" never intended by this term the universally predicated existence which is conceived by the mind. For such an existence is but an accident among others occurring in association with the realities of things. That is to say, these realities are the substance, whereas that existence which is conceived by the mind, the universally predicated existence, is but an accident associated with them.

order.why: Read the relation between elements, composition, and existing beings.
Retain the philosophical criticism rather than assuming all accounts agree.
Read the objection about absolute nothingness as part of an argument.
Consider why absolute nothingness cannot be an existing thing.
Keep the further reported argument about conceiving nothing.
Distinguish essential origination from transformation in time.
shortened: The pre-existence of God is both essential and temporal, while the origination of the contingent world is essential but not temporal, as we have already explained another day at table.

But matter and the universal elements cannot be entirely destroyed and annihilated.  No, their annihilation is merely transformation.  For instance, when man dies his body becomes dust, but it does not become absolute non-existence:  it retains a mineral existence, but a transformation has taken place and that composition has been subjected to decomposition.  It is the same with the annihilation of all other beings, for existence does not become absolute non-existence and absolute non-existence does not acquire existence.

order.why: Read the reported account of atoms and nonannihilation.
Compare another reported statement about continuance.
Examine the different senses of eternity in the material example.
Return to the familiar flower and relative coming and going.
shortened: So this flower, this hyacinth, was for a time coming from non-existence into existence and is now passing from existence into non-existence.

order.why: Consider continuous grace and beginningless life.
Read the reported interpretation of Genesis in its own setting.
shortened: Moses teaches: "In the beginning, God created heaven and earth. And the earth was deserted and empty, and it was dark in the depth and the spirit of God floated above the water. And God said: there shall be light! and there was light, etc." Here nowhere is written that God created the world of out nothing. Nothingness should be the antithesis, the opposite, of God. The answer to that however is: "In the beginning of the creation of the world, God emanated the heaven and the earth.

order.why: Distinguish a prior possibility from an existing personal consciousness.
Keep the short reported statement about potentiality in that context.
Consider how the passage distinguishes spirit from matter.
Recognize that a term for divine existence cannot contain its referent.
shortened: His existence is true existence which is self-subsistent, not an intellectually perceived and comprehended existence; it is an Existence by which all created things come into being.

We refer to Him as Self-Existent because we need to make use of a term but we do not mean that that Being can be contained within our comprehension. What is intended is the Reality from Whom all things emanate, the Reality through Whom all things exist.

order.why: Explains contingency, existence and quiddity, and creation from absolute nonexistence.
Move into the devotional language of dependence and poverty.
shortened: For verily I and all else, as encompassed by Thy knowledge, are but utter nothingness in the depths of contingency and the seas of creation, and absolute poverty that hath perished. How then can one whose limit is that of non-existence and evanescence describe the Sovereign of pre-existence and invisibility?

order.why: Read creation from nothing within the prayer’s register.
shortened: Thou didst bring me forth from utter and absolute nothingness into the realm of being and existence, and honored me with the glory of beholding Thy presence--the highest aspiration of all Thy Prophets and chosen ones.

order.why: Follow the prayer’s movement from deprivation to gifts.
shortened: How can we render thanks that He brought us into being from nothingness, bestowed the spirit of existence upon us when we were utter void, granted us divine manifestation when we were sheer nothingness, guided us to the fountain of life when we were thirsting, clothed us in the garment of "Blessed be God, the Best of Creators" when we were naked, gave us direction when we were wandering, led us to His shelter when we were lost, granted seeing eyes when we were blind, bestowed hearing when we were deaf, gave us eternal life when we were dead, and granted spiritual freshness and grace when we were withered.

order.why: Consider the worth given by relation to the divine.
shortened: All that comes within one's imagination as well as all that appearance in external reality whether potential or actual existence all are in truth absolute non entities, they are nothing itself except that which is to be related to the Ancient Beauty or which can be attributed to His Holiness our Merciful Lord.

order.why: Read waves and ocean alongside the enduring divine face.
shortened: The world of existence is like an ocean and these determined beings are its waves. Although they have existence and visibility, they are considered non-existent and lost, except for the sacred realities of divine souls. Although they too are determined beings, yet being illumined from the praised station and assisted from the extended shadow, they attain eternal realization in the world of existence and find everlasting determination. This is the meaning of "All things perish save His face."

order.why: Bring the inquiry into striving for a fuller life.
shortened: O candle of the love of God! In this world of nonexistence, in which existence is only an appearance, strive to obtain real existence; in this dark world, endeavor to shine out as a luminous candle; and in this constricted arena, seek a vast and spacious domain.

order.why: Consider the aspiration toward an enduring name.
shortened: Since thou art a servant of the Eternal and a seeker of the Face of God and fleeing from extinction, follow not the setting star and seek not that which vanisheth. Seek thou that which is eternal, everlasting and sempiternal, and that which is perpetual, endless, and without peer or likeness - so that thou mayest truly be Abdul-Baqi (Servant of the Eternal) and a servant of the Everlasting Lord.

order.why: Close the linked readings with the gift of spiritual life.
shortened: O thou who art gladdened by the fragrances of God!

In this mortal dust-heap, every nostril that becomes perfumed with the divine breaths hath received a portion from the realm of pre-existence and gained a share from the bounty of God's immortal kingdom of being. Otherwise, alas for us! Woe unto us! The hours of all would be fruitless, the foundation carried away by the wind, and manifest loss would appear.

order.why: Preserve the supplied account of relative existence.
Compare the provisional rendering on essential and temporal beginnings.
End with the supplied Augustine passage on different kinds of priority.

questions: How can the same thing be described as real in one relation and as nothing in another?
What is clarified by distinguishing a beginning in time from dependence upon a cause?
Where do the chair, moonlight, and sound-and-song examples help, and where do their limits become apparent?
How does the meaning of nothingness change between philosophical arguments and prayers in this compilation?
What difference might an acknowledgement of dependence make to gratitude, responsibility, or the search for understanding?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the spiritual meanings of self-effacement and endurance.

references.label: 1 · Augustine, Confessions, XII.29.40 · Priority without an interval of time
references.note: Augustine distinguishes priority by eternity, time, preference, and origin. Sound is the material of a song, yet the singing does not first emit an unformed sound and subsequently turn it into a tune. Compare this distinction with essential and temporal origination here, while retaining Augustine’s own account of divine creation.

subjects.displayTitle: Divine names: recognition, praise, and the life we lead
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh pictures His own name the Concealer turning back to the Most Holy Court in sorrow because it has seen a believer exposing another’s faults, and the name the All-Forgiving grieving over a transgression it was forced to witness. To invoke mercy and speak unkindly is a contradiction the names themselves feel. From that moral shock the inquiry widens: the Imam tells Hishám that bread is the name of what is eaten and not the thing itself, so that worshipping a name alone is worshipping nothing; the Báb calls the names mirrors in which nothing is seen but the Sun; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that we call God all-knowing not to measure Him but to deny Him any imperfection, and that every attribute we can praise is met in the Manifestations, who reflect what the Essence forever withholds. The Qur’án’s permission to call upon God as Allah or as the Merciful, joined to counsel on the very voice of prayer, keeps naming tied to practice [1]. The path continues toward the oneness of God, the unknowable transcendence behind every name, and the gentler country of forgiveness, grace and mercy where the names ask to be lived.
subjects.arc: Begin with the ethical demand of the names, examine how language and manifestation disclose without enclosing, and return through prayer to qualities that benefit the world.

order.why: Consider attributes as signs in the visible world.
shortened: As to the attributes and perfections such as will, knowledge, power and other ancient attributes that we ascribe to that Divine Reality, these are the signs that reflect the existence of beings in the visible plane and not the absolute perfections of the Divine Essence that cannot be comprehended.

order.why: Open with the names protesting conduct that contradicts them.
Distinguish the name from the named through the bread example.
shortened: He who worshippeth the name without the reality hath indeed disbelieved and worshipped naught. He who worshippeth both the name and the reality hath indeed committed polytheism and worshipped two. But he who worshippeth the reality without the name - this is true unity.

Were the name identical with the named, each name would be a god. But God [...] these names, and they are all other than He. O Hisham! 'Bread' is the name for that which is eaten, 'water' is the name for that which is drunk, 'garment' is the name for that which is worn, and 'fire' is the name for that which burns.

order.why: Explore verbal, written, and living forms of names.
shortened: The truth in all stations is as Ali, peace be upon him, hath said: "The name is the mark of a thing," and it hath ranks. Among them is the name in realities, which in all its ranks is like a living being, such as man, indicating the named one. Among them are mirrors which indicate what is reflected in them through them. Among them are verbal names, inscribed names, angelic names, horizonal names, and names of the self, and among them is everything upon which the name of a name falls.

order.why: Read the names as gifts for worship rather than definitions enclosing God.
Distinguish traces that guide from attachment to those traces.
Follow knowledge through the image of the sun and its effects.
Read attributes as denying imperfection and appearing in the Manifestations.
shortened: But no soul has ever fathomed the reality of the Essence of the Divinity so as to be able to intimate, describe, praise or glorify it. Thus all that the human reality knows, discovers and understands of the names, attributes and perfections of God refers to these holy Manifestations and leads nowhere else: "The way is cut off, and all seeking rejected."

Yet we ascribe certain names and attributes to the reality of the Divinity and praise Him for His sight, His hearing, His power, His life and knowledge. We affirm these names and attributes not to affirm the perfections of God but to deny that He has any imperfections.
When we observe the contingent world we see that ignorance is imperfection and knowledge is perfection, and thus we say that the sanctified Essence of the Divinity is all-knowing.

order.why: Distinguish knowledge of qualities from comprehension of Essence.
Keep the detailed argument concerning names and divine unity.
Consider simplicity and the manifestation of many names.
Read the relation between attributes and Essence.
shortened: Thus, the attributes are specifications that exist in the essence but are not distinguished from it. They are seen and unseen.

order.why: Explains divine names as negations of imperfection and as attributes manifested through the Manifestation.
Keep divine knowledge distinct from created knowledge.
Consider the attributes beyond dependence on created conditions.
Read the many names in relation to oneness and Quran 17:110.
shortened: But in the world of contingence when the lights of Its perfections and qualities shine these lights reflect in the mirrors of names and attributes but all names and attributes are in relation to that Essence in the same station. "Whatever Name ye may call Him He is the possessor of All Beautiful Names" [Q17:110], whether Manifest or the Manifester, whether the Seer or the Seen One, whether the name the Unseen whether the Present One.

order.why: Explore the stations of names as mirrors.
shortened: All the names thou seest or examples thou witnesseth are signs that God hath created for the exaltation of the Manifestation of His Self and the inaccessibility of the Dawning-Place of His Being.

Say: The sea of names is two seas wherein ye traverse, seeing naught but God. Say: The names are like mirrors - do ye see aught but the Sun therein? Say: Glory be to God! Naught is seen therein save God. All call upon God, their Lord, by His names.

order.why: Read their reference to the Primal Word.
shortened: In this station, He was and ever shall be sanctified beyond all mentions and names, and exalted above the understanding of all created things. The way is barred and the quest forbidden. Therefore, whatever wondrous mentions and exalted descriptions flow from the tongue and pen refer to the Most Great Word, the Supreme Pen, the Primal Point, the true Home, and the Dawning-Place of the All-Merciful Revelation. He is the Source of unity and the Manifestation of the light of oneness and detachment.

order.why: Distinguish manifested names from the transcendence they signify.
shortened: Say:  Lordship is My Name, whereof I have created manifestations in the world of being, while We Ourself remain sanctified above them, would ye but ponder this truth.  And Godhead is My Name, whereof We have created exponents whose power shall encompass the people of the earth and make them true worshippers of God, could ye but recognize it.  Thus should ye regard all Our Names, if ye be endued with insight.

order.why: Consider the Manifestations as mirrors of attributes.
shortened: These Tabernacles of holiness, these primal Mirrors which reflect the light of unfading glory, are but expressions of Him Who is the Invisible of the Invisibles. By the revelation of these gems of divine virtue all the names and attributes of God, such as knowledge and power, sovereignty and dominion, mercy and wisdom, glory, bounty and grace, are made manifest.

Therefore, these illuminated Souls, these beauteous Countenances have, each and every one of them, been endowed with all the attributes of God, such as sovereignty, dominion, and the like, even though to outward seeming they be shorn of all earthly majesty.

order.why: Read creation as adorned with names through the Dawning-Place of signs.
Read First, Last, Hidden, and Manifest in the passage’s own theological account.
shortened: The Point in Its Primal station of Firstness hath ever been, and will continue forever to be. He is more true and befitting to be praised by all Names, than the praise of any Name for Itself.

For He is the First at the time that He is the Last, and He is the Hidden at the time that He is the Manifest, and He is the One Who is praised by all the Names, at the very time that He is glorified above the praise by any Name.

order.why: Follow the further manifestation of divine names.
Consider names as signs leading toward recognition.
shortened: All names are but attributes of His Will, and all attributes are but descriptions of His Purpose, that the servants might know their Creator and describe Him according to what He hath revealed unto them through them, that "there is no God but Him" - the Single, the One, the Eternal. Nothing comprehendeth Him and nothing is associated with Him.

order.why: Introduce the relationship between attributes and eternal creation.
shortened: And regarding proof for the temporal eternity of contingent beings in this transient world - briefly, divine sovereignty is eternal, and the existence of beings is from the eternal effulgences of the Sun of Reality. One cannot imagine the sun without rays. All divine names and attributes are eternal, and their requirements are also eternal.

order.why: Examine the creator–creation and teacher–pupil arguments.
Read the reported reasoning from phenomena to attributes.
Consider the objects upon which attributes are expressed.
Retain the reported examples of generosity and sovereignty.
shortened: If you hear one is a king, who has neither subjects nor territory, how can it be proved that he is a king? He must have the preparation and other necessaries before he can rightly be called a king. Thus the attributes of God proved the necessity of creation. Some may say the attributes of God were preexistent, but god did not use them. This would be like the generous without generosity; the merciful without mercy. The attributes of God could not be delayed.

order.why: Keep the reported comparison across dispensations in its own terms.
Read the universal call under the King of names.
Consider the claim concerning the revelation of all names.
shortened: As to what thou didst write concerning the unveiling of the names and attributes - by God! We have rent asunder the veils and torn away the shrouds on the Day when We manifested Ourselves with all names unto all things. Blessed are they that behold! Blessed are they that know!

order.why: Read the warning that names can become veils.
shortened: Tear ye asunder the veils of names and cleave ye their kingdom. By My Beauty! He Who is the Monarch of all names is come, He at Whose bidding every single name hath, from the beginning that hath no beginning, been created, He Who shall continue to create them as He pleaseth. He, verily, is the All-Powerful, the All-Wise.

order.why: Retain the passage on the Most Great Name and its supplied omission.
Keep the further account of the names’ reach within its source limits.
Read the prayer and its account of names without imposing an explanation on its numerical details.
shortened: Thine are the Most Beautiful Names in their essence and the Most Exalted Examples in their abstraction.

I testify, and all Thy creation testifieth, that unto Thee belong all the Most Beautiful Names - their first and their last, their manifest and their hidden - and the Most Exalted Examples in their essence, their pristine nature, their simplicity and their abstraction.

order.why: Connect invocation with the reception of bounty.
Hear the names invoked for healing, preservation, and forgiveness.
shortened: Glory be to Thee, O Lord my God! I implore Thee by Thy Name, through which Thou didst lift up the ensigns of Thy guidance, and didst shed the radiance of Thy loving-kindness, and didst reveal the sovereignty of Thy Lordship; through which the lamp of Thy names hath appeared within the niche of Thine attributes, and He Who is the Tabernacle of Thy unity and the Manifestation of detachment hath shone forth; through which the ways of Thy guidance were made known, and the paths of Thy good pleasure were marked out; through which the foundations of error have been made to tremble, and the signs of wickedness have been abolished; through which the fountains of wisdom have burst forth, and the heavenly table hath been sent down; through which Thou didst preserve Thy servants and didst vouchsafe Thy healing; through which Thou didst show forth Thy tender mercies unto Thy servants and revealedst Thy forgiveness amidst Thy creatures -- I implore Thee to keep safe him who hath held fast and returned unto Thee, and clung to Thy mercy, and seized the hem of Thy loving providence.
Thou art, verily, the Healer, the Preserver, the Helper, the Almighty, the Powerful, the All-Glorious, the All-Knowing.

order.why: Close with names as gateways to benefit, order, education, and life.
shortened: Each of His names is a gateway to blessing, mercy, grace, bounty, protection and generosity, and the effects of each have been and continue to be the cause of order in the world and the preservation of nations. Through His name the Educator, He hath educated and continueth to educate the world, and in the Perspicuous Book He hath called Himself the Lord of all worlds.
Through His name the Quickener, the breath of life was breathed, and through His name the Powerful, other effects appeared...

questions: How does the opening passage connect the names we invoke with the way we speak and act?
What is gained by distinguishing a name, a sign, and the reality to which they point?
How do these selections relate the unity of God to the multiplicity of divine attributes?
What does Quran 17:110 contribute to reflection on the relationship between theological language and the practice of prayer?
How might sustained attention to one divine name change an ordinary relationship or responsibility?

neighbors.invitation: Consider recognition through attributes and signs.

references.label: 1 · Quran 17:110 · Beautiful names and the manner of prayer
references.note: The verse permits invocation as Allah or the Merciful, affirms the divine possession of beautiful names, and counsels a middle course in the voice used for prayer. Compare its joining of naming and practice with the compilation’s ethical and devotional treatment of attributes. The linked page provides seven translations for comparison.

subjects.displayTitle: The limits of comprehension and the possibility of discovery
subjects.introduction: A flower may know nothing of the person who stands beside it, and its ignorance changes nothing about that person’s existence. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá returns often to this quiet observation because it unsettles a common assumption, that whatever lies beyond our perception must be unreal. The stone cannot conceive of growth, the plant cannot imagine sight, the animal cannot enter the world of intellect; each, if it could speak, would deny the kingdom above it. The unborn child, too, has no notion of the world awaiting it. Yet the teaching is not a counsel of resignation. Rational evidence, signs in creation and the growth of the spirit open real if partial windows, and the soul that rises beyond this life will see what it now only infers. Paul writes of things no eye has seen being made known through the Spirit [1], a kindred hope. Such humility steadies the mind for further steps: toward the way the higher embraces the lower, toward the limits of language and intellect, and toward the unknowable Essence of God.
subjects.arc: Begin with the difference between ignorance and nonexistence, examine the analogies and their limits, and turn toward signs, reason, and the promise of fuller understanding.

order.why: Open with the flower whose ignorance does not disprove humanity.
State the distinction between inability to perceive and nonexistence.
Develop that distinction through the mother and child.
shortened: Man's spirit comprehends the realities of kingdoms which have no knowledge of him, even as the child in the womb has no knowledge of exterior existence; nevertheless, the mother comprehends the child's existence. The superior kingdom understands the inferior, but that the inferior comprehends it is no proof of the non-existence of the superior kingdom. In the human world, if we do not understand the divine world, is that a proof that the world of God does not exist?

order.why: Introduce the accessible image of rooms above and below.
Read the flooring example as an analogy about capacities.
shortened: We are created; likewise, this plant is existent, this mineral exists, this wood exists. But can this flooring here comprehend those who are standing upon it? It cannot, because sight and hearing are properties or faculties belonging to a higher kingdom than the mineral. The difference between these two kingdoms, the vast difference between the mineral kingdom and the human kingdom, is a hindrance to comprehension.

order.why: Consider different forms of life sharing one world.
shortened: For example, the mineral life occupieth its own plane, but a mineral entity is without any awareness at all of the vegetable kingdom, and indeed, with its inner tongue denieth that there is any such kingdom. In the same way, a vegetable entity knoweth nothing of the animal world, remaining completely heedless and ignorant thereof, for the stage of the animal is higher than that of the vegetable, and the vegetable is veiled from the animal world and inwardly denieth the existence of that world---all this while animal, vegetable and mineral dwell together in the one world.

order.why: Read the Tablet to Dr Forel’s account of degrees of comprehension.
shortened: Minerals, plants and animals are bereft of the mental faculties of man that discover the realities of all things, but man himself comprehendeth all the stages beneath him. Every superior stage comprehendeth that which is inferior and discovereth the reality thereof, but the inferior one is unaware of that which is superior and cannot comprehend it.

order.why: Follow the detailed sequence through the kingdoms.
shortened: The mineral kingdom, for example, which is lower, is precluded from comprehending the vegetable kingdom; for the mineral, any such understanding would be utterly impossible. In the same way, no matter how far the vegetable kingdom may develop, it will achieve no conception of the animal kingdom, and any such comprehension at its level would be unthinkable, for the animal occupieth a plane higher than that of the vegetable: this tree cannot conceive of hearing and sight. And the animal kingdom, no matter how far it may evolve, can never become aware of the reality of the intellect, which discovereth the inner essence of all things, and comprehendeth those realities which cannot be seen; for the human plane as compared with that of the animal is very high.

order.why: Distinguish development within a degree from grasping another.
shortened: That which exists in a lower rank cannot comprehend, much less inquire about, that which exists in a rank above it. Consider the ranks of mineral, plant, animal and man. However much the mineral might progress to the zenith of its perfection, it can never comprehend the reality of the plant, nor its attributes and perfections; rather its ascent and progress remain within the realm wherein it was created, according to that rank and station.

order.why: Compare the concise formulation of that barrier.
shortened: Moreover, differences of degree in the world of creation are a barrier to knowledge. For example, as this mineral belongs to the mineral kingdom, however far it may rise it can never comprehend the power of growth. The plants and trees, however far they may progress, cannot imagine the powers of sight or of the other senses. The animal cannot imagine the human degree, that is, the spiritual powers. Thus, differences of degree are a barrier to knowledge: the inferior degree cannot comprehend the superior.

order.why: Retain the reported hierarchical account of creation.
Read the brief reported summary.
shortened: That which is lower cannot perceive the higher. The mineral cannot understand or feel the plant; plants cannot understand or perceive the animals; and animals cannot comprehend man.

order.why: Pause at the tree’s lack of access to human experience.
Follow the longer reported comparison of faculties.
Keep the reported relation between animal perception and human spiritual life.
Read the contrast among kinds of ground in its supplied context.
Retain the racialized historical report for critical examination, not as a classification of peoples.
Read the polemical comparison concerning denial of immortality critically.
shortened: Similarly the animal, steeped in the faculty of sense perception does not comprehend the world of intellect. In its own language it cries out: where is the world of intellect? In like manner the unspiritual man denies the Immortality of the soul. Why? Because he is living in an inferior degree. Just as the cow denies the existence of the intellect the materialist negates the immorality of the soul.

order.why: Consider the further reported contrast of worlds of consciousness.
shortened: For even as the plant imagines life ends with itself and has no knowledge of our existence, so the materially-minded man has no knowledge of other worlds of consciousness.

order.why: Turn from created degrees to the question of the essential Reality.
shortened: It is a self-evident fact that phenomenal existence can never grasp nor comprehend the ancient and essential Reality. Utter weakness cannot understand absolute strength. When we view the world of creation, we discover differences in degree which make it impossible for the lower to comprehend the higher.

order.why: Read the limitation of degree as an argument about knowing.
shortened: Assuredly this is an absolute impossibility, for when we study the creational world, we see that the difference of degree is a barrier to such knowing. An inferior degree can never comprehend a higher degree or kingdom.
The limitation of an inferior degree is the barrier to comprehension.

order.why: Distinguish contingent reality from the Absolute.
shortened: Although the mineral, vegetable, animal and human are all realities of this world, the difference between their stations prevents the lower from comprehending the higher. In view of this, how could a contingent being comprehend the reality of the Absolute?

order.why: Consider the distance between creature and Creator.
shortened: We observe that every lower thing is incapable of comprehending the reality of that which is higher. Thus, no matter how far they may evolve, the stone, the earth and the tree can never comprehend the reality of man or imagine the powers of sight, hearing, or the other senses, even though the former and the latter alike are created things. How then can man, a mere creature, comprehend the reality of the sanctified Essence of the Creator?

order.why: Retain the concise reported question about comprehension.
shortened: All superior kingdoms are incomprehensible to the inferior; how therefore could it be possible that the creature, man, should understand the almighty Creator of all?

order.why: Turn toward manifest signs while acknowledging the limits of thought.
shortened: ...the reality of Divinity in its fullness cannot be comprehended within human capacity, for that which proceeds from minds and thoughts is limited while the reality of Divinity is unlimited. What is clear and evident are His manifest signs which have set the world of being in motion. But the reality of Divinity is sanctified and exalted above the comprehension of all created things.

order.why: Read the seeker’s heart and the inaccessible divine abode.
shortened: For were they to reach the ultimate object of their quest for God and their attainment unto Him, they would have but reached that abode which hath been raised up within their own hearts. How then could they ever hope to ascend unto such realms as have not been ordained for them or created for their station? Nay, though they journey from everlasting to everlasting, they will never attain unto Him Who is the midmost Heart of existence and the Axis of the entire creation, He on Whose right hand flow the seas of grandeur, on Whose left stream the rivers of might, and Whose court none can ever hope to reach, how much les His very abode!

order.why: Consider the limits of comprehending the Word of God.
shortened: No lower thing can comprehend what is above it - just as the stone and tree, no matter how much they progress, cannot comprehend the reality of the animal, and the animal, no matter how much it progresses, cannot comprehend the reality of man. Thus man, no matter how much he progresses, cannot fathom the reality of the Word of God.

order.why: Keep the reported distinction between prophetic mirrors and the divine Essence.
Preserve the explicit place of rational evidence.
shortened: Every being lower in the scale of creation is incapable of comprehending the stages transcending its own.

By the same reasoning, when we consider the human kingdom, we realize that man is incapable of perceiving the world of the soul, which an immaterial reality. He has no knowledge thereof save through rational evidences. But when we enter the world of the spirit, we will see that the soul unquestionably exists, and that it is a luminous and eternal reality.

order.why: Read the womb analogy as a promise of knowledge beyond present conditions.
shortened: Similarly is man's condition in the womb of this world. When he hastens to the other world, he observes that he has been delivered from a narrow and dark world and has entered into the divine world. If in this merciful existence that universal spiritual existence remains unknown and unrecognized, let there be no wonder or astonishment, for every lower realm is unaware of the higher realm, just as the fetus in the womb is unaware of this world. When it transfers to the higher world it becomes aware and perceives, but before transfer, conception and comprehension are impossible.

order.why: Consider the spiritual meaning of the worlds described.
shortened: Concerning what occurreth after man ascendeth from this contingent world to the realm of the placeless - all the conditions of Heaven and Hell are spiritual in nature, although that world is not separated from this world. Its separation, in truth and meaning, is like the separation of the human kingdom from the kingdom of the mineral, for the mineral is unaware of the human world.

As for the unveiling of the beauty of the Holy Manifestations at the time of ascending to the limitless worlds, this pertaineth to the fact that the world of physical senses and material perceptions is metaphorical while the world of the spirit is reality itself.

order.why: Read the soul’s further understanding while retaining the source omission.
shortened: When the soul of man ascends to the bountiful realm, it certainly unveils this physical world, for every higher station unveils the station below it, but a lower station cannot unveil a higher station.
But the mineral world has no knowledge of man's pure world.

order.why: Explains why lower stations can know the higher only through its self-manifestation in their own being.
Close the linked readings with the reported possibility of assistance.
Keep the provisional formulation separate from verified source passages.
Compare the supplied womb analogy in its own wording.
End with the supplied connection between fuller understanding and good works for departed souls.
shortened: When the soul of man ascendeth to the world of heavenly bestowals it will certainly lift off the veil from this material world, for every higher state comprehendeth the states inferior to itself. An inferior state, however, is incapable of grasping the reality of whatever transcendeth its station.
Charitable deeds and good works performed on behalf of departed souls will certainly have a beneficial influence.

questions: How does the flower example distinguish a limit of perception from evidence of nonexistence?
What can the analogies of kingdoms, rooms, and the womb clarify, and what would they be unable to establish by themselves?
How do the passages leave room for rational evidence and inquiry within acknowledged limits?
How does Paul’s account of knowledge through the Spirit compare with the accounts of signs and future understanding here?
How can we read the polemical and racialized historical examples critically while refusing to turn spiritual language into a ranking of peoples?
What habits would help us remain both open to discovery and careful in judging claims about what we cannot presently perceive?

neighbors.invitation: Ask how language serves an understanding it cannot fully contain.
Explore the capacities and limits of human inquiry.

references.label: 1 · 1 Corinthians 2:9–12 · Knowledge received through the Spirit
references.note: Paul moves from the limits of ordinary seeing and hearing to knowledge given through the Spirit, using an analogy with a person’s knowledge of their own inner life. Compare this with the distinction between what exceeds present perception and what may be known through signs or spiritual development. The respective accounts of revelation retain their theological differences.
